description.narrative:
To take major steps towards a European export ban on highly hazardous pesticides, we are connecting organisations worldwide and closely coordinating our strategies.
1. In South Africa and Brazil, we are strengthening groups and coalitions that are fighting against pesticide use in national movements: activists, farm workers, conservationists and farmers who want to raise awareness among consumers in their own countries, convince politicians to announce an import ban and ban dangerous toxins from theirfields and crops. Inthis project, Oxfam Novib partners Women on Farms Project (WFP) in South Africa and Confederação Nacional dos Trabalhadores e das Trabalhadoras Assalariadas Rurais (CONTAR) in Brazil are given the means to bring these groups together,to (continue to) drive a movement, to conduct research and to run joint campaigns.
The possibilities in both countries differ: in South Africa, there is scope to fight for an import ban on pesticides that are banned in the EU, while in Brazil, the agricultural industry still has so much power in parliament that this is not feasible within the project period. That is why we are working with CONTAR to broaden support for aban on highly dangerous pesticides. In this way, we are laying the foundations for a possible import ban in the future.
2. In the Netherlands, we are bringing together food, environmental and farmers' organisations that currently often work separately or in temporary coalitions to promote toxin-free food. We are combining our research, lobbying power, networks and supporters to push supermarkets, the Dutch government and the EU to take effective action. Oxfam Novib is using its years of experience with successful supermarket campaigns to launch a new, strong campaign together with all these organisations. Time and again, our approach to supermarkets – a combination of talks with retailers and well-thought-out public campaigns – has proven to be effective in getting this sector to take action.
Our first (Green Saint Nicholas) campaign in 2006 mobilised 100,000 people: seven major retail chains promised tosell only fair trade chocolate letters. Building on Behind the Brands (2013-2017), in which hundreds of thousands of consumers urged the ten largest food giants to improve their policies on labour rights, land rights and climate, we organised Behind the Barcodes from 2018 onwards. In this international campaign, in which millions of customers bombarded their supermarkets with petitions, tweets, emails and actions at shops, we once again held large chains to account on human rights and sustainability. On that basis, we negotiated with the retailers, made concrete recommendations and, after four years, saw significant improvements in the policies of Lidl and Aldi in the Netherlands and, to a lesser extent, at Jumbo, Albert Heijn and PLUS.
In the Netherlands, we continued our supermarket work with the Superlijst Sociaal (Social Superlist), together with Questionmark and Solidaridad. Before publishing our scores,we gaveretailers the opportunity to improve their policies, which three large chains did. In the recent cocoa campaign, our survey of the five largest Dutch supermarkets showed that only 5.6% of the cocoa in all their chocolate products is fair trade. Fair means that farmers receive a living income for an agreed period of time ( ). We found a pioneer in Albert Heijn, which was the first supermarket in the world to commit to paying a fair price to cocoa farmers for all its own-brand chocolate products. We are now discussing with other supermarkets how they can follow this good example.
In Ban the Poison Boomerang, we are once again mobilising consumers through accessible campaigns, using the research and stories of our partners. Together, we are asking supermarkets not only to ban toxins from their shelves and chains, but also to help their smaller suppliers – financially and with training, for example – to produce toxin-free products, both in the Netherlands and abroad. Furthermore, we want supermarkets topublicly support legislation for an export ban, as Ahold Delhaize did last year when, encouraged by Oxfam, it explicitly declared its support for European anti-diverting legislation (CSDDD). Previously, companies such as AS Watson Benelux (Kruidvat, Trekpleister, ICI Paris XL) and supermarket chain Ekoplaza also advocated for IMVO legislation after discussions with us. This kind of support from pioneers is crucial to counterbalance the enormous lobbying power of the agrochemical industry in Brussels.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam International is a confederationorganisations working together in more than 94 countries to find lasting solutions to poverty, suffering and injustice. Oxfam Brazil is one of them. With many of the causes of poverty global in nature, members of Oxfam International believe they can achieve greater impact in addressing issues of poverty by their collective efforts.To achieve the maximum impact on poverty, the Oxfams link up their work on development programs, humanitarian response, lobbying for policy changes at national and global level. The Oxfams popular campaigns and communications work is aimed at mobilising public opinion for change. Oxfam Brazil is a global and Brazilian civil society organization that works together with and mobilizes people, groups, organizations and institutional bodies. It makes political alliances, encourages the convergence of actors, provides financial support, conducts research, produces, disseminates and brokers knowledge, informing public opinion and mobilizing citizens and organizations to leverage change. It wants to change the conditions that generate and perpetuate inequality and poverty, while respecting the sustainability of the planet.
